Silbo Gomero is a whistled language spoken on the island of La Gomera in the Canary Islands, used by shepherds and fishermen communities to communicate across long distances that would be inaudible if spoken normally. It encodes Spanish phonologically but in whistled form, allowing speakers to communicate over distances of one to two kilometers. The language works through pitch and duration variations in the whistle that encode Spanish consonants and vowels, with different whistle pitches corresponding to different phonemes. The language developed in isolation on La Gomera as a practical tool for rural communities separated by deep valleys, with shepherds and agricultural workers using it for coordination. By the nineteen eighties, Silbo Gomero was nearly extinct as younger generations abandoned shepherding and rural life, leaving only a few hundred fluent speakers remaining. The language narrowly escaped extinction through deliberate cultural preservation. It was revitalized through UNESCO recognition in 2001 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage and formal reintroduction to school curricula in the two thousands, and it is now taught systematically to maintain the tradition. Related whistled languages exist in other parts of the world, including a Zapotec whistled speech in Mexico and whistled languages in Papua New Guinea and a few other communities, though Silbo Gomero remains the most documented and institutionally supported whistled language, demonstrating that language can be transmitted in non-vocal channels while preserving structural phonological features.
